title: Cooneen Ghost House: Ireland's infamous cottage linked to alleged paranormal activity
excerpt: The chilling story of Fermanagh’s Cooneen Ghost House, where a family was reportedly terrorised by unexplained paranormal activity.
content:
Situated in the isolated townland of Cooneen, near the Fermanagh-Tyrone border, the Cooneen Ghost House is at the centre of one of Ireland's most infamous paranormal stories.

The derelict cottage, associated with the Murphy family, has been the subject of local folklore for more than a century, following reports of unexplained disturbances that allegedly terrorised a widow and her children in the early 1900s.

In 1911, Bridget Murphy was living at the property with her six children when the family began experiencing a series of strange occurrences.

What initially appeared to be unexplained knocks, footsteps in the empty loft and unusual noises soon escalated into more frightening incidents.

According to accounts of the haunting, plates moved across tables, bedclothes shifted in empty beds and loud banging and rapping could be heard throughout the cottage.

Some of the noises were reportedly heard in the rhythm of familiar tunes, including 'The Boyne Water' and 'The Soldier's Song'.

The alleged disturbances attracted considerable attention from the local community, clergy and even politician Cahir Healy, who became involved in efforts to investigate the claims.

Father Coyle, a Catholic priest from Maguiresbridge, was among those who visited the property.

Accounts of the time described pots and pans banging together, strange shapes appearing on the walls and other unexplained activity.

As the family's distress continued, Bridget sought help from the Church, with Father Coyle receiving permission to carry out two exorcisms at the cottage.

However, the rituals reportedly failed to bring an end to the disturbances. Accounts claimed that bedsheets lifted into the air, crockery flew around the rooms and loud groaning noises came from upstairs during the attempts.

Rumours subsequently circulated about the possible cause of the alleged haunting, including claims that one of the Murphy children had discovered a book entitled 'The Legions of Doom' in nearby woodland.

The book was said to contain instructions for performing satanic rituals and contacting spirits, with speculation that attempts to summon a supernatural presence had triggered the events.

The family reportedly faced suspicion and hostility from some neighbours as the stories spread.

In 1913, the Murphy's decided to leave Ireland and emigrate to America, but accounts of the haunting claim the disturbances followed them aboard the ship.

Reports described banging and moaning noises coming from the family's cabin during the voyage, allegedly disturbing other passengers and prompting the captain to intervene.

The story of the Cooneen Ghost House has endured as part of Fermanagh's folklore, with the abandoned cottage continuing to attract the interest of paranormal enthusiasts and visitors.

In recent years, the removal of surrounding forestry trees by the NI Forest Service has brought the building back into view, exposing the isolated stone structure that had long been hidden among the woodland.

The haunting has also featured in television coverage, including the BBC series 'Northern Ireland's Greatest Haunts'.

During the programme, spiritual medium Marion Goodfellow described experiencing what she believed was an angry male presence and an overwhelming sense of negative energy inside the property.

She reportedly described it as one of the scariest and most awful places she had ever visited.

More than a century after the Murphy family left Cooneen, the cottage remains a source of fascination, with its history of alleged paranormal activity continuing to fuel one of Ireland's best-known ghost stories.
